resources.string: Larger bubble text during a shift
Choose which delivery apps gig.log reads. Shift tracking works only in apps gig.log fully supports.

Saves your full history as spreadsheet files in a folder you choose:
deliveries.csv: one row per delivery
sessions.csv: one row per shift
summary.csv: totals and estimated IRS mileage deduction
expenses.csv: logged expenses, including undone ones
fuel.csv: logged fill-ups, including undone ones

The files include store names, your expense labels as you typed them and gig.log's tracked miles at each fill-up. Customer names and addresses, which gig.log keeps only as codes, are left out. gig.log doesn't upload them, but a cloud folder may. The files stay after you uninstall; delete them from the folder. Exporting again replaces them.
Exported %1$d files to the chosen folder.
Export failed (%1$s). Check the folder and try again.

Saves a bug report, giglog-bug-report.txt, to a folder you choose. It lists the app\'s main events, like offers and deliveries. gig.log replaces known private details first but can miss some, so read it before sharing. gig.log doesn\'t send it to the developer; a cloud folder may upload it. It stays after uninstall; delete it from the folder. Exporting again replaces it.
Exported giglog-bug-report.txt. Private details removed from %1$d lines.
Bug report export failed (%1$s). Check the folder and try again.
Each automatic tap stays off until you allow it, and gig.log asks again when its instructions for finding that button change. Your own Accept and Decline presses work either way.
No automatic taps yet. They show up when a delivery app supports them.
When %1$s asks you to confirm a decline, gig.log taps Decline again for you, after checking the label. Works only with Quick declines on in Offer rules.
Not used yet. gig.log has no automatic accept or decline, so this choice changes nothing today.
After a %1$s delivery, gig.log taps the arrow that opens the pay details, so it can record them. The arrow has no label, so gig.log checks only that it is in %1$s.
Offers carry a Protect acceptance rate note. Nothing is tapped for you.
When off, shopping offers carry a Shopping off note. Nothing is tapped for you.
After you tap Decline, gig.log taps the confirm button. Needs your OK under Automation & Consent.
Drag to reorder. Rules higher up count more.

Off unless you turn it on. A screenshot is saved only when this switch and its type below are on; the types start on.

A screenshot shows the whole screen, including customer details, other apps and anything else showing, like a video or the keyboard. It goes to Pictures/gig.log. gig.log never uploads it, but gallery sync or sharing can. Screenshots stay after you uninstall; delete them in your gallery.

None is taken if this switch is off or another app is in front at that moment; one already saving still finishes. This switch doesn't affect your shift history.
Which app the bubble shows when two delivery apps are online. In every mode, cards and the chat header name their app.
Shows the delivery app you used last. A pick in the bubble\'s switcher holds until that app\'s shift ends, then the bubble follows again.
Your switcher pick stays until you change it, even across that app\'s next shift. While that app is offline, the bubble shows the app you used last.
Test mode: one stack of cards from every app with a live shift, each labeled with its app. No switcher; the chat follows the app you used last.
Optional. gig.log still works without it, using screen changes from the delivery apps only.

gig.log gets a signal from every app when its screen changes. It reads and saves screens only from the delivery apps you turn on; of other apps it sees only the name. Screenshots, if you turn them on, save the whole screen, including any app behind an offer.
Lets gig.log catch an offer that pops up over another app.
In this test build, screen reading turns itself off and the app can\'t be used until you allow them again.
On Android 11, this may not take effect.
See which other app is open

If this phone\'s census ID has signed up with the server, gig.log first asks the server to delete its census data, and resets only once the server confirms; until then nothing is reset. The reset forgets the census install ID and secret, deletes the waiting outlines and captures, and turns capture sharing off. The next upload signs up a new install ID, which the census server must trust again. The census switch stays as it is.
The census server hasn\'t confirmed deleting this phone\'s data yet, so the ID can\'t be reset.

Sends the text of screens gig.log doesn\'t recognize to the census server while the server trusts this install. These screens get only the general privacy filters, so a capture can still hold customer details that the server\'s operator can read.
Highlights the bubble\'s Odometer button early in a shift, and after one until you log a reading

Screens of the delivery apps you turn on, through Android Accessibility. Those apps\' notifications; other apps\' are skipped unread. GPS during a shift. Gas-price lookups use your last location each time they run (daily when automatic, in setup for each fuel type while automatic updates are on, and when you refresh it or choose Use auto price in the bubble), even off shift. Screen reading and calculations happen on your phone. Recognized banking, payment and ID screens, the ID camera and the signature pad are dropped unsaved. The filters work in English and can miss a screen.
With Screen events on, also the name of the app in front.

Customer names and addresses in your history are saved as codes, so gig.log can tell customers apart without knowing who they are. Store names and addresses are saved as text. Screenshots are pictures and keep everything on screen.

From the screens and notifications it recognizes: shifts, offers, deliveries and pay. From what you enter: expenses, fill-ups, cash tips, notes, odometer readings, corrected shift miles, vehicles, your goal and settings. Also the miles GPS counted, and a log of main events that keeps only recent entries.

gig.log has no account and no ads ID, and includes no outside analytics code. Gas-price lookups: Android\'s address lookup may send your location, rounded to about 11 km, to its provider to find your region, and the U.S. Energy Information Administration gets a price request for that region, with no account or install ID. Daily updates are off on a new install, and an update keeps your setting; to stop them, set the bubble\'s gas price to manual, or turn off daily updates in setup and save. Vehicle lookup starts after you tap \"Look up my vehicle\". gig.log saves that choice. The year, make, model and EPA vehicle ID you pick go to fueleconomy.gov, with no account or install ID. \"Search Google for MPG\" opens Google with the year, make and model. Spoken offers go to your phone\'s text-to-speech engine, which may use the network. Exports go to the folder you choose, and a cloud folder may upload them; spreadsheets leave out customer codes, and bug reports replace known private details but can miss some.

Off unless you accept it in Settings > Data & privacy > Census, which first shows what it sends. When on, it sends gig.log\'s census server, at most once a day, outlines of the screens and notifications gig.log doesn\'t recognize, at most one of each layout a day, and daily counts of the screens it recognized, from the delivery apps you pick, with this install\'s ID, over HTTPS. Each day it picks a random time to send; a send waits up to an hour for Wi-Fi (unless you allow mobile data) and battery, and is skipped that day if it can\'t start by then. The choice is saved on this phone with its date, app version, privacy notice version and the census server\'s address, together with the delivery apps and Wi-Fi setting you pick. That record leaves the phone only in a bug report you export. If the server\'s address changes, the census stays off until you accept again. The census screen lists what gig.log sent in the last 7 days, a list kept on this phone only, and can ask the server to delete what it holds for this phone; until the server\'s next update, that request waits on the phone. The server keeps this phone\'s census ID, a tally of today\'s uploads for 7 days, and data it can\'t tie to this phone; its backups keep the rest for up to 14 days.

Off unless you accept the invitation. gig.log shows it only after a shift ends, and only on a phone that has been on the census for 8 days, recorded 2 shifts and ran a shift on 3 of the last 7 days. gig.log works that out on the phone; to accept, it sends the census server a yes, never the counts. The server gives this phone a reviewer permission for 30 days, and gig.log asks again when it ends. While you review, the server keeps a log of which screens gig.log asked it about, tied to that permission, for up to 30 days. After a shift, the screens to review show what gig.log would send, with the customer and account details it can detect covered; the words it may show stay in the phone\'s memory, never in its storage, and are gone when gig.log restarts. A confirmation sends the word\'s one-way code. The word itself is sent only after the census server reports that at least 2 phones confirmed it and enough phones see it. A label sends which field it is, never the field\'s value. Ask the developer arrives in a later update. Stopping, turning the census off or deleting your census data ends the permission. Your answer is saved on this phone with its date, app version and privacy notice version, and leaves the phone only in a bug report you export.

Your history, settings and consent choices are kept in gig.log\'s private storage on the phone, which other apps can\'t read, and Android encrypts that storage. gig.log adds no encryption of its own. Gas-price and vehicle lookups and the census use HTTPS, and gig.log refuses unencrypted connections. Screenshots and exports are ordinary files outside that storage, so apps you let see your photos or files can read them.

Off unless turned on in Settings > Data & privacy > Screenshots. A picture of the whole screen, including customer details and any app behind an offer, saved to Pictures/gig.log. gig.log never uploads it; gallery sync or sharing can. It stays after uninstall until you delete it.
Android backup and phone transfer may copy your history and settings and restore them. Consent choices and logs are left out, so a new phone asks again.

Until you delete it. Settings > Data & privacy > Delete everything on this phone deletes your history, settings, consent choices and logs; with the census on, it first asks the census server to delete its data and shows whether the server confirmed. Clearing app data or uninstalling also deletes it. A backup can bring it back on a reinstall or a new phone. Logs keep only recent entries. Screenshots and exports stay until you delete them.

Each choice on Automation & consent is saved on this phone with its date, app version and privacy notice version. The app log notes each automatic-tap choice. Both leave the phone only in a bug report you export.

This test build saves the text of the delivery apps\' screens and notifications on the phone. On screens it recognizes, its rules replace the customer details they know about; elsewhere the filters can miss them. Its log also keeps screen text. That text stays until removed or uninstalled, and backup and transfer leave it out. Capture sharing, off unless turned on in developer options, needs the census and the server\'s trust; it sends the text of unrecognized screens, never notifications, and the server\'s operator can read it. Screen events are required: without them, screen reading turns itself off and the app can\'t be used.
Outlines of unrecognized screens, off by default
The census server changed, so uploads stopped. Turn the census on to accept again.
When off, uploads can use mobile data

Settings > Data & privacy > Delete everything on this phone deletes what gig.log keeps on the phone, and asks the census server first. The 30-day limit and deleting the census server\'s data take effect with the census server\'s next update; until then a deletion request waits on this phone.

This test build can also send the text of unrecognized screens from a phone the census server trusts, with capture sharing on in developer options. The 30-day limit doesn\'t apply to it yet. Deleting the census server\'s data takes effect with the census server\'s next update; until then a deletion request waits on this phone. Settings > Data & privacy > Delete everything on this phone deletes what gig.log keeps on the phone, and asks the census server first.
Before you turn on the census
The census is off unless you accept. gig.log works the same with it off.

Outlines of the delivery apps\' screens and notifications that gig.log doesn\'t recognize. An outline keeps the screen\'s layout and replaces each word with a code made by a one-way function, a fingerprint the server can\'t turn back into the word. The server can still recognize the code of a common word by trying that word. Amounts, clock times, distances, minutes and item counts go as their format, such as $#.##, never the value. Before coding, gig.log leaves out words that look like a name or an address; the filters can miss a name, which then goes only as a code. The screen as you see it is never sent. With the outlines go daily counts of the screens gig.log recognized, by delivery app and app version.
Delivery apps change their screens, often in some areas before others. Outlines from phones in other areas let gig.log keep recognizing screens after a change.
gig.log\'s census server, at %1$s. The server also sees the phone\'s IP address during each upload.

At most once a day. gig.log picks a random time each day to send. A send waits up to an hour for Wi-Fi, unless you allow mobile data in the census settings, and for enough battery, and is skipped that day if it can\'t start by then. Uploads are encrypted (HTTPS).
Linked to this phone for 30 days
Uploads carry an ID for this phone, so the server can tell uploads from the same phone apart for 30 days, and not after.
You can turn the census off at any time, and delete from Settings the census data the server holds for this phone and everything gig.log keeps on the phone.
Your agreement with a delivery company is between you and that company.
Reviewing is separate from the census, and off unless you accept. The census works the same either way.
Ask the developer arrives in a later update.
After a shift, gig.log may show you a few screens it didn\'t recognize, at most 3 a day. Customer details and your own account details that gig.log can detect are covered before you see a screen.
Confirm that a word on a screen is the delivery app\'s own wording, such as \"Pick up by\", and label what a field is, such as tip or deadline. Ask the developer about a screen you\'re unsure of.

A confirmed word goes as its one-way code. The word itself is sent only after other drivers confirm the same word. A label goes alone, without the field\'s value. Ask the developer sends the screen\'s outline as the review shows it; only the developer can open it, and the census server deletes it after 3 days.

To accept, gig.log sends the census server a yes, never your shift counts. The server gives this phone a reviewer permission for 30 days, and gig.log asks again when it ends. While you review, the server keeps a log of which screens gig.log asked it about, tied to your reviewer permission, for up to 30 days.
You can stop at any time on this screen. Stopping, turning the census off or deleting your census data ends the permission, and reviews waiting on the phone are dropped.
Reviewing is on. The permission ends %1$s.
gig.log couldn\'t reach the census server. Try again later.
gig.log is still sending your census deletion request. Try again once the server confirms it.
This phone has no census ID yet. It gets one with its first census upload.
The census server takes reviewers once this phone\'s census ID is 8 days old. gig.log asks again after a later shift.
The census server didn\'t accept this phone as a reviewer.
The census server stopped reviews from this phone, so gig.log sends nothing for reviews.
Your reviewer permission ended after 30 days. Accept to review again.
Deleting your census data ended your reviewer permission.
Turning the census off ended your reviewer permission.
This phone\'s census ID changed, which ended your reviewer permission.
The census server no longer holds a reviewer permission for this phone.
The census server stopped accepting this phone\'s census ID, so the census is off and reviewing ended.

Reviews open to a phone that has been on the census for %1$d days, recorded %2$d shifts and ran a shift on %3$d of the last %4$d days.

Each upload the census server received in the last 7 days, read from what gig.log sent. This list stays on this phone. Codes are words sent as one-way codes. Formats are values sent as their format, such as $#.##. Type only is a number or longer text sent as its type alone. Left out is what the filters held back.

Requested. gig.log sends the request when the phone is online, and uploads nothing until then.
Requested. The census server can\'t take deletion requests until its next update; gig.log keeps asking, and uploads nothing until then.
Requested. The census server couldn\'t confirm this phone\'s ID; gig.log will retry, and uploads nothing until then.

resources.string: No deletion was sent: this phone had no census ID at the time.
This phone\'s census ID can no longer be used, so gig.log couldn\'t send the request.

gig.log deletes the outlines and daily counts waiting on this phone, then asks the census server to delete the uploads it can tie to this phone. This doesn\'t turn the census off; turn it off to stop later uploads.

Some data stays. The server keeps this phone\'s census ID, so later uploads still work, and a tally of today\'s uploads (counts, and an ID for each upload so a repeat isn\'t stored twice), which it keeps for 7 days. It can\'t tie the rest to this phone: outline samples stored without this phone\'s ID, totals across all phones, words already approved because many phones sent them, rules and made-up test screens already published, and older records whose link to any phone has been destroyed.
Server backups made before your request keep this phone\'s records until they expire, at most 14 days later. If the server is restored from one, it deletes them again before it serves anything.
History, settings, consent choices and logs
gig.log deletes every shift, delivery and offer it recorded, your vehicles and plans, your settings and consent choices, its logs, and any captures of screens it didn\'t recognize.
First it asks the census server to delete what it holds for this phone, and shows whether the server confirmed.
Files you exported, screenshots in your gallery and any Android backup of gig.log in your Google account stay, because they\'re kept outside gig.log.
gig.log then closes. Open it again to set it up from the start; every automatic tap and the census stay off until you allow them again.
Waiting for an upload to finish
A census upload is running. gig.log deletes nothing until it finishes.
gig.log couldn\'t save the decision to delete, so nothing was deleted. Try again.
Waiting for the census server to confirm it deleted this phone\'s data
The census server confirmed it deleted the uploads it can tie to this phone.
The census server didn\'t answer in time.
gig.log couldn\'t reach the census server.
The census server can\'t take deletion requests until its next update.
The census server couldn\'t confirm this phone\'s census ID.
This phone\'s census ID can no longer be used, so gig.log can\'t ask the census server to delete its data.
If you delete now, gig.log can\'t ask again, and the census server keeps this phone\'s uploads until they age out. The 30-day limit takes effect with the census server\'s next update.
If you wait, nothing is deleted. gig.log keeps asking, and the census screen shows when the server confirms; then delete everything here.
Android didn\'t clear gig.log\'s storage. Clearing it in Android\'s Settings > Apps > gig.log deletes the same data.
